title: 1 Samuel: the heart God sees

lines: First Samuel carries Israel from the judges to the kings through three lives. Samuel, the answer to a childless woman's prayer. Saul, the first king. And David, anointed in secret.
It's a book about power: who holds it, and how it's given.

scripture.text: The LORD sends poverty and wealth; He humbles and He exalts.

lines: It moves in seven stages. Samuel's birth and call. The ark lost and returned. Israel asks for a king. Saul's reign and rejection. David at Saul's court. David the fugitive. And the end of Saul.
The three lives overlap, and the handover is never clean.

scripture.text: Thus far the LORD has helped us.

chapters.kicker: Watch for: the boy who listens
lines: The book begins when the word of the LORD was rare, and it becomes the story of a prophet through whom God speaks.
Speak, for Your servant is listening.
Kings stand or fall by whether they listen. Hearing and obeying count above sacrifice.

scripture.text: Speak, for Your servant is listening.

chapters.kicker: Watch for: give us a king
lines: The elders ask for a king like all the nations. God calls it a rejection of his own rule, and then gives them one all the same.
Readers weigh why. The question the book asks is whether the king will rule as a servant under the word of God.

scripture.text: they have rejected Me as their king.

lines: People keep judging by what they can see. Saul is a head taller than anyone. Samuel is taken with Jesse's tall eldest son. God looks somewhere else.
For man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart.
And David is chosen from the sheepfold.

scripture.text: For man sees the outward appearance, but the LORD sees the heart.

lines: Jonathan, Saul's heir, gives up his claim out of love for David and trust in God's choice. And twice David has Saul in his power and won't harm him.
It teaches restraint and trust in God's timing. It doesn't teach silence before injustice.
The command against Amalek in chapter fifteen is read in more than one way, and none of them makes it easy.
On every reading, no people living today is Amalek, and no one may use this chapter to justify violence or contempt toward any person or people.
Start with Hannah's song in chapter two, slowly. Then the key chapters: three, four, eight, fifteen, sixteen, seventeen, and twenty-four.
Don't take its heroes as models in everything.
Then read Second Samuel. The promise to David is still ahead.
